newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gold mines trade fees for brighter future.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gold mines trade fees for brighter future.

text.p: Many South African mining houses are scrapping the traditional and complicated system of management contract fees in a move which could raise the value of the country's gold shares in foreign investors' eyes.
Analysts said on Wednesday that many South African gold mines could in future be freed from paying dues to the sovereign mining houses and instead be allowed to appoint their own management.
This would improve the ratings of South African gold shares, which are currently under-valued by international standards, they said.

"Management contracts are no longer a poison pill. Foreign mining companies will at last be able to try their luck in South Africa. This could do nothing but good for ratings of South African gold shares," Julian Baring of Mercury Asset Management wrote in an article in local newspaper Business Day.
Last week, Gencor Ltd and Anglovaal Ltd, as part of their respective restructurings, arranged to cancel the management contracts that they have with their mines.
Gencor is to merge its four Evander gold mines and Anglovaal is to group its gold mining assets into Avgold.
As a result the mines will no longer have to pay management fees to their mining house, but instead manage themselves or contract out -- possibly cutting costs, analysts said.

Investec Fergussons mining analyst John Clemmow told Reuters that cancelling management contracts -- the terms of which are seldom revealed to shareholders -- would make the South African mining business vastly more transparent.
Analysts said that individual mines would benefit from contract cancellations as fees would become part of their distributable income and so reveal a clearer income picture.
Shareholders in the individual mines would also have a more direct and focused management, they said.
"Management fees are distinctly a problem. Now the income of the mine would accrue to it. The process will be more transparent and would probably cost less," Clemmow said.
Baring applauded the cancellation of contracts but challenged the fees Gencor and Anglovaal planned to charge shareholders for scrapping management contracts they had never voted for.
Both mining houses agreed to install independent, non-executive directors at their mines, so bringing management in line with that of international mining companies.

"I believe that independent directors can do nothing but good for the mines, especially if some are from overseas," said Baring, whose Mercury Gold and General Fund has 47 percent of its portfolio invested in South Africa.

Baring said that allowing mines to choose their own management would converge interests of mines and mining houses who hold them because it would be in the house's best interest to maximise the individual mines' share price.
Instead of earning income from management fees, the houses would earn dividends from successfully managed companies.
Clemmow said that Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd -- the world's largest gold miner -- would be unlikely to cancel management contracts.
But JCI Ltd and Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd were likely to, he said. -- Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482-1003
